newsitem.title: USA: GM wants faster developments from suppliers.
newsitem.headline: GM wants faster developments from suppliers.

text.p: General Motors Corp.'s top purchasing executive delivered a stern message to suppliers Friday: cut new technology development time in half or lose our business.

Harold Kutner, vice president of GM's worldwide purchasing, also told suppliers at a conference here that they will be expected to fix parts causing warranty problems by a certain time or face financial penalties.

"If someone can't bring us a system in 12 months instead of 18 months, then they won't win the business, regardless of what they have to offer," Kutner told reporters after his speech to suppliers at their annual meeting at the University of Michigan.
GM, the world's largest automaker, spends $70 billion a year to buy components and systems from about 12,000 suppliers worldwide.
Kutner said suppliers in general have improved from the early 1990s, starting to cut costs to compete on a global basis. "The supply industry is very successful today," he said.

But GM still has parts that take too long to make, according to Kutner. Some suppliers take 74 weeks to bring a vehicle's front bumper and grille from design approval to production. Seats take 142 weeks, while heating-ventilation and air conditioning systems take 153 weeks, he said.

By contrast, Chrysler Corp. said this week it cut eight months off the development time of its new LH large cars to 31 months. Chrysler made the leap by using more efficient platform teams and computer technology to simulate prototypes.

GM needs more help from suppliers as it seeks to improve its relationships with consumers, Kutner said. When a parts problem arises, GM has a new programme to meet with the supplier to determine what the defect is.

If it is the supplier's fault, Kutner said the component maker will have 90 days to fix the problem. The supplier will receive a financial reward for beating the deadline and will be penalised if it is not met.

Some suppliers said the changes GM is imposing were likely to be met with scepticism. One supplier questioned Kutner about how a company can be held responsible for a part that it made to GM's specifications.

David Andrea, an analyst at Roney & Co., said GM itself plays a big role in how well suppliers can cut development time on new parts and components. "That's as much up to the manufacturer as it is the supplier," Andrea said.

Kutner also said suppliers in Asia and the Pacific region often supplied better parts than those in North America. For instance, 80 percent of suppliers in Australia have hit a zero parts-per-million defect level.
GM is continuously looking for new suppliers and is serious about a deadline for large suppliers to boost quality by the end of 1997, he said.
"Those suppliers who don't meet that won't get our business," he said.
Separately, GM said it cut its vehicle production schedule for the third quarter from levels announced last month because of production losses from recent strikes in Pontiac and Warren, Mich.
GM's stock fell $1.31 to $62.69 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
